name: Casein protein

lead: Casein is the main protein in milk and is sold as a powder. It digests slowly, which is why bodybuilders and forum users take it before bed.
It is a food-grade protein, not a drug. Evidence relates to muscle protein, not to facial or aesthetic changes.

paras: In the stomach casein forms a gel and releases amino acids over several hours, compared with the faster absorption of whey.
Main concern is milk-protein allergy or intolerance. Otherwise it is a common food ingredient sold without prescription.

lead: Casein is the main protein family in milk, making up roughly 80% of cow's milk protein, and is sold as a powdered supplement (commonly micellar casein or calcium caseinate) in the bodybuilding and fitness market [1][2]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly as a slow-digesting protein taken before bed to support muscle mass.

The reasoning behind the use is that casein forms a gel in the stomach and releases amino acids gradually over several hours, in contrast to whey, which is absorbed faster [1][2]. Proponents therefore pair whey after training with casein at other times, particularly overnight.

Published human work on casein as a muscle supplement consists largely of small exercise trials; a registered 2025 trial compared pre-sleep and post-exercise casein in 24 participants [3]. Casein is a common food allergen in a small share of children, and people with milk protein allergy or intolerance avoid it [1].
infobox: Forms a gel in the stomach; slow amino acid release [1]

paras: Casein is a group of related phosphoproteins (alpha-S1, alpha-S2, beta and kappa types) that makes up about 80% of the protein in cow's milk and a smaller share (about 20 to 60%) in human milk [1]. In milk it exists as spherical colloidal particles called micelles held together by calcium and hydrophobic interactions [1][2]. Casein precipitates at about pH 4.6, which is why it curdles in an acidic stomach and in cheesemaking [1][2].

Commercial forms include sodium and calcium caseinates, used widely as food emulsifiers and stabilisers, hydrolysed casein, in which enzymes have partly broken the protein down, and micellar casein, which keeps the natural micelle structure and is the form usually sold in sports tubs [1].

In the stomach casein clots into a gel that releases amino acids into the blood slowly, sometimes over several hours [1]. Hydrolysed casein is digested faster than intact casein [1]. Casein supplies essential amino acids along with calcium and phosphorus [1][2]. Reference texts describe it as a high-quality protein with a high leucine content [2].

Users describe casein as a pre-sleep protein intended to supply amino acids overnight and limit muscle protein breakdown, usually alongside whey after training [4]. One looksmax.org thread argues for taking casein roughly 80% of the time and whey around workouts, and adds the claim that dairy raises IGF-1 [4].
Some users in the same discussion say casein is harder to drink than whey, and others ask about vegan powders as cheaper alternatives [4].

Cow's milk protein allergy affects an estimated 0.25 to 4.9% of young children, with limited data for adults; heat-treated casein may be more allergenic [1]. Casein-containing products are unsuitable for people with milk-protein allergy [1]. Casein and gluten-free diets sometimes used for autistic children have weak supporting evidence for behavioural benefit [1].

A separate debate concerns A1 versus A2 beta-casein variants; a 2005 independent review and a 2009 European Food Safety Authority review found no identifiable link between A1 milk and chronic disease [1].

Registered human studies include a completed 2025 trial comparing casein taken before sleep with casein after exercise in 24 people [3], trials of casein with leucine in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [5][6], and a trial of casein versus a whey-based supplement with exercise in older adults [7]. These registrations do not themselves report outcomes in the sources reviewed here. Most studied populations are athletes, older adults or patients rather than people seeking aesthetic changes, and no study reviewed here tests casein for facial or bone-structure appearance.
